name: CCTV
basis: surveillance video: block compression, held frames, clock, motion box (how)
note: Barrel lens and sensor noise are device physics, but the look is defined by digital compression and overlays; the tracking box is subject-aware.

lumenary.blurb: Seen by a security camera: a wide lens, a few frames a second, blocky video compression, a clock that keeps counting, and a box that locks onto whatever moves. A still picture is watched too, and the detector picks out the busiest part of it.

facts.era: Closed-circuit television from the 1940s, digital recorders from the 1990s
facts.bestOn: Wide scenes with a figure or object away from the middle

why: Security video looks the way it does because of what it is for: to record a lot, cheaply, for a long time. A wide lens sees the whole room, a slow frame rate and heavy compression keep the files small, and a cheap sensor fills the dark with noise. None of it is meant to be beautiful, which is why it reads as evidence, and why a gentle portrait run through it suddenly feels like something caught.
how: Bend the picture with a barrel lens so the middle swells and the corners pull in and darken.
Wash the colour out, or turn it to grey or to the green of night vision, then add sensor noise and a flicker of the gain.
Take a new frame only a few times a second and hold it in between.
Flatten each small block of the frame towards its own average colour, and now and then let a block fail to update.
Score a coarse grid by how much changed there, or how busy the picture is, and draw a tracking box round the best cluster.
Stamp the camera name, a running clock and a blinking REC dot over the top.
history: Closed-circuit television was first used in Germany in 1942 to watch rocket launches from a safe distance, and spread to banks and shops in the 1960s. Tapes were reused until they wore out, which gave the grainy, smeared look. Digital recorders in the 1990s replaced tape with block-based compression, whose square artefacts became the new signature. Motion detection, which records only when the picture changes, followed soon after and is behind the boxes drawn over the footage in modern systems.
uses: Album art and lo-fi music videos
Social posts that look like caught evidence
terms: A lens effect in which straight lines bow outward and the middle of the picture swells.
A small square of a compressed video frame that is stored and updated as a unit.
The amplification of the sensor signal; more gain brightens a dark scene and adds noise.
paragraphs: The lens is a lookup table built once for the picture size. For a pixel at offset d from the centre, measured in half diagonals, the picture is read at the point d / f, where f = 1 - 1.6 k r^2 + 0.1 k, r is the distance from the centre and k is 0.55 times the lens slider. Because f falls towards the corners, the lookup there reaches farther out, so the corners are pulled in and the middle swells: barrel distortion. The same table holds a vignette that darkens with r, more strongly for a stronger lens. Colours are read from the nearest pixel, as a cheap sensor would.

Each camera frame is built pixel by pixel: the colour is washed to 55% saturation, or turned to grey, or mapped to a green ramp from (l - 110) x 1.45 + 120, then multiplied by the vignette and a flicker factor and added to noise taken from a hash of the pixel and the frame number. Compression then works on blocks about W/80 pixels wide: each block is pulled towards its mean by a factor that falls from 1 to 0.22 as the compression slider rises, and with probability 0.045 Q^2 a block keeps its previous contents. A new frame is made only every 1/fps seconds, and between frames the last one is shown with every other line darkened by 12%, for interlacing.

The tracking box comes from a grid 20 cells wide. On a video each cell sums the colour change since the last camera frame; on a still picture it sums the strength of the edges (a Sobel filter). The grid is blurred by one cell, the highest cell is found, and the box is the bounding box of the cells within three of it that score above 45% of it. The box moves 40% of the way to its target at every camera frame, so it follows smoothly. On a still picture the detector swaps to the second best place every 3.2 seconds.

equations.tex: f=1-1.6\,k\,r^{2}+0.1\,k,\qquad \mathbf p_{\text{src}}=\mathbf c+\frac{\mathbf p-\mathbf c}{\max(0.35,\ f)}
equations.note: The barrel lens: r is the distance from the centre in half diagonals and k is 0.55 times the lens slider.
Compression: every pixel of a block moves towards the block average; Q is the compression slider (0 to 1).
The chance, at each camera frame, that a block keeps its old contents.

presets.text: Night vision with heavy compression turns any picture into a grainy infrared recording.
Slow the camera to three frames a second and strengthen the lens for an old lobby feed.
Switch off the overlay and the box to keep only the look of the video itself.
